passages.original: Problemata ergo et propositionea (ut dictum est) derminata sint. Positio est opinio admirabilis alicujus familiarium secundum philosophiam,utquod non estcuntradicere,quemadmodum dixit Antisthenes, et quod omnia moventur, secundum Heraclitum, aut quod unum est ens, quemadmodum Melissus dixit(nam de quovis contraria opinionibus profarenle curam habere stultum est, aut de quibus orationem habemuscontrariam opinionibus, ut quoniam non omne quod est, vel factum est, vel aeternum, quemadmodum sophistae dicunt.
passages.english: Let problems and propositions, then, be defined (as has been said). A thesis is a paradoxical opinion of someone well known in philosophy, for example that it is not possible to contradict, as Antisthenes said, and that all things are in motion, according to Heraclitus, or that being is one, as Melissus said (for to concern oneself with just anyone who puts forward [views] contrary to [common] opinions is foolish); or [a thesis concerns] things about which we have an argument contrary to [common] opinions, for example that not everything that exists either has come to be or is eternal, as the sophists say.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'propositionea' for 'propositiones', 'derminata' for 'determinata', 'cuntradicere' for 'contradicere', 'profarenle' for 'proferente'. The parenthesis opened at 'nam de quovis' is not closed in the text; I have closed it after 'stultum est'.

passages.original: Eligere autem oportet et ex scriptis disceptationibus. Descriptiones autem facere in unoquoque genere supponentes seorsum (ut de bono;:aut de animali, et de bono omni) incipientem a quid est. Adnotare autem et singulorum opiniones, ut quod Empedocles quatuor dixit clementa corporum esse. Ponet enim aJiquis quod ab aliquo probato dictum est. Sunt autem (ut figurali- ter sit complecti) propositionum et problematum partes tres ; nam aliae sunt morales propositiones, aliae naturales, alix rationales.
passages.english: One should also make selections from written discussions, and draw up outlines in each genus, setting them out separately (for example about the good, or about animal, and about every [kind of] good), beginning from 'what it is'. One should also note down the opinions of individuals, for example that Empedocles said there are four elements of bodies. For someone will grant what has been said by some approved person. There are (to put it in outline) three parts of propositions and problems: for some propositions are ethical, others natural, others logical.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'clementa' read as 'elementa', 'aJiquis' as 'aliquis', 'alix' as 'aliae', 'figurali- ter' as 'figuraliter'. 'Rationales' is rendered 'logical' (Greek logikai).

passages.original: Nam omne quod participat genus, vel species, vel individuum est:difrerentia autem neque individuum, neque species;manifestum igitur quoniam non participat genus differentia,quare neque impar species erit,sed differentia, quoniam non participat genus. Amplius,si genus in specie posuit,ut contiguitatem idipsum quod est continuitatem, aut mixturam idipsum quod est temperamentum,aut (ut Plato definivit) lationem secundum locum mutationem : non enim necessarium contiguitatem continuitatem esse, sed e converso continuitatem contiguitatem, non enim omne contiguum continuatur, sed quod continuatur contiguum est.
passages.english: For everything that participates in a genus is either a species or an individual; but the differentia is neither an individual nor a species. It is evident, therefore, that the differentia does not participate in the genus, so that 'odd' will not be a species either, but a differentia, since it does not participate in the genus. Further, [see] if he has placed the genus in the species, as [saying] that contact is the very thing that continuity is, or that mixture is the very thing that blending is, or (as Plato defined [it]) that locomotion is change with respect to place. For it is not necessary that contact be continuity, but conversely that continuity be contact; for not everything in contact is continuous, but what is continuous is in contact.

passages.original: Si igitur et in hoc oportet admittere quod aer motus est spiritus, non tamen de omnibus hujusmodi est assignandum,de quibus non verificatur genus,sed de quibuscunque vere prædicatur assignatum genus,nam in quibusdam non videtur verificari, ut in luto et nive, nam nivem dicuntesse aquam coagulatam,lutum autem terram humido temperatam : est autem neque nix aqua,neque lutum terra,quare neutrum assignatorum generum erit genus.Oportet enim genus verificari semper de omnibus speciebus.Similiter autem neque vinum est aqua putrefacta(sicut Empedocles dicit:In ligno putruit unda),nam simpliciter non est aqua.
passages.english: If, then, one must admit in this case too that wind is air in motion, still [the genus] must not be assigned in all such cases where the genus is not true [of the species], but [only] in those of which the assigned genus is truly predicated. For in some cases it does not seem to be true, as with mud and snow. For they say that snow is congealed water, and mud earth mixed with moisture; but snow is not water, nor is mud earth, so that neither of the assigned genera will be a genus. For the genus must always be true of all the species. Likewise wine is not rotted water either (as Empedocles says: 'In the wood the water rotted'), for it is not water without qualification.
passages.notes: 'Spiritus' here means wind or breath (Greek pneuma). The Empedocles quotation refers to water fermenting into wine in the wood, that is, in the vine.

passages.original: ut scientiam indeciduam,terram autem nutricum,aut temperantiam consonantiam, nam omne obscurum,quod secundum metaphoram dicitur,contingit et etiam metaphora loquentem calumniari,tanquam non proprie dicentem, non enim congruetdictadefinitio, ut in temperantia,nam omnis consonantia in sanis.Amplius,si est genus con- sonantia temperantiæ, in duobus generibus erit idem, non continentibus se invicem,nam nequeconsonantia virtutem, neque virtus continet consonantiam. Amplius, si non positis nominibus utitur, ut Plato ciliurabre oculum, aut araneum putrimordax, aut medullam ossigenium dixit, nam omne obscurum, quod insuetum est.Qusedam autem neque secundum xequivocationem,nequesecundum metaphoram,neque proprie dicuntur, ut les, mensura, vel imago eorum quae natura justasunt;sunt autem hujusmodi deteriora metaphora.nam metaphora facit quodammodo notum quod designatum est per similitudinem (umnesenimmetaphora utentes,secundum aliquam similitudinem ea utuntur), at quod tale esi,non facitnotum,nam neque similitudoestsecundumquam mensura,vel imago lex est,neque dici solet proprie;
passages.english: for example [calling] knowledge 'unshakeable', the earth a 'nurse', or temperance a 'concord'. For everything said by metaphor is obscure. It is also possible to cavil at one who speaks in metaphor as not speaking literally; for the stated definition will not fit, as in the case of temperance, for every concord is in sounds. Further, if concord is the genus of temperance, the same thing will be in two genera that do not contain one another, for neither does concord contain virtue, nor virtue contain concord. Further, [see] if he uses words not in established use, as Plato called the eye 'brow-shaded', or the spider 'poison-biting', or the marrow 'bone-generated'; for everything unusual is obscure. Some things are said neither by equivocation, nor by metaphor, nor literally, as [saying] that law is the 'measure' or 'image' of things just by nature. Such expressions are worse than metaphor; for metaphor in some way makes what is signified known through the likeness (for all who use metaphor use it according to some likeness), but what is of this sort does not make [anything] known; for there is no likeness according to which law is a measure or an image, nor is it customarily said literally.
passages.notes: Scanning corruptions: 'ciliurabre' presumably for 'ciliumbrem' (Greek ophruoskion, 'brow-shaded'); 'putrimordax' for Greek sēpsidakes ('putrefying-bite' or 'poison-biting'); 'in sanis' read as 'in sonis' (in sounds); 'xequivocationem' for 'aequivocationem'; 'les' for 'lex'.

passages.original: Amplius, si similibus nominis casibus similes orationis casus aptantur,ut si adjutivum est effectivum sanitalis,adjutive est sanitatis effective, et1adjuvansefficiens sanitatem.Considerandumiet in idea,si aptabitur dictus terminus. Nam in quibus- darE non accidit,ut quernadmodum Plato definivit, mortale addens in animalium definitionibus, idea enim non erit mortalis, ut ipse homo ; quare non aptabitur ad ideam definitio. Simpliciter autem in quibus apponitur efl'ectivum aut passivum,necesse est dissonare in idea terminum,nam impassibiles et immobiles videntur esse ideæ iis qui dicunt ideas esse ;
passages.english: Further, [see] if similar inflections of the account are fitted to similar inflections of the name, for example if 'beneficial' is 'productive of health', [then] 'beneficially' is 'productively of health', and 'benefiting' is 'producing health'. One must also consider whether the stated definition will fit the Idea. For in some cases it does not happen, as when Plato defined, adding 'mortal' in the definitions of animals; for the Idea will not be mortal, e.g. man-himself; so the definition will not fit the Idea. And in general, wherever 'productive' or 'passive' is added, the definition necessarily fails to accord with the Idea, for the Ideas seem to be impassible and immovable to those who say that Ideas exist;
passages.notes: 'adjutivum' etc. render Greek ōphelimon ('beneficial'). Scanning errors corrected ('sanitalis', 'quernadmodum', 'efl'ectivum').

passages.original: Si vero alterius opinionem tutetur respondens, manifestum quoniam ad illius intelli- gentiam aspiciendo,ponere singula debetet negare; quare et qui curant extraneas opiniones (ut bonum et malum esse idem,quemadmodum Hpraclitus inquit,) non dant non adesse simul contraria eidem, non videntur eis haec,sed quia secundum Heraclitum sic dicendum.Faciunthoc autem et qui suscipiuntab invicem positiones ; conjectant enim ac si is dicat qui ponit. Manifestum igitur quae conjectandum respondenti, sive simpliciter probabile, sive alicui positum est.
passages.english: But if the answerer is defending someone else's opinion, it is evident that he ought to grant or deny each point by looking to that person's thinking. Hence also those who adopt foreign opinions (for example that good and bad are the same, as Heraclitus says) do not grant that contraries are not present together in the same thing, not because these things seem [so] to them, but because according to Heraclitus one must speak thus. Those also do this who take up theses from one another; for they aim at what the one who posits [the thesis] would say. It is evident, therefore, what the answerer must aim at, whether what is posited is generally reputable or reputable to some [particular] person.
passages.notes: 'conjectant' rendered 'aim at' (Greek stochazesthai). The clause 'non videntur eis haec' is elliptical; I have supplied 'not because'.
